text.en: The two menorah parshiyos reflect two aspects of the menorah: as one vessel of the Mishkan it belongs to the whole building, but as Torah it is a mitzvah of its own that functions even where the building is not complete or no longer stands.
'Outside the paroches' is not a negative instruction where not to place the menorah, but a statement that the menorah belongs even outside, even when the Mikdash is destroyed.
The ner maaravi parallels the Kosel Maaravi: precisely in the west, where the sun of Israel sets, there remains a light that is never extinguished, the essence of Torah.
Moshe's name being hidden in Tetzaveh is his reward, not his punishment: one hides what one wants to preserve, so the man who offered to be lost for Israel is preserved as the hidden light.
Moshe's 'erase me' stands against Amalek's erasure: because he was ready to be erased so that Israel would exist, he is present in every war against Amalek until Moshiach.

Moshe's plea to enter Eretz Yisrael was, in one explanation, a wish to intercalate the year, which means making the lunar year equal to the solar year, so that Knesses Yisrael, the moon, would be equal to the sun.

The Jews declined to make Purim a yom tov because a yom tov, like Shabbos, has no poor and lacks nothing, while they wanted a day of matanos l'evyonim, which draws Hashem's blessing to Knesses Yisrael even in galus.

Yocheved's renewed youth was not only a miracle for her: since Moshe's soul comes from the source of all renewal, a flow of chiddush came down with his birth, and his first mitzvah to Israel was Kiddush HaChodesh.

Three times establishes a habit, so by the third Rosh Chodesh after the Exodus its newness should have faded; the Torah was given precisely then, teaching that Torah must stay as new as Rosh Chodesh itself.
Water is always a plural word because it has no defined form or single essence, while Moshe, the greatest form in the world, is unique, as 'there arose no prophet like Moshe'.

The astrologers rightly sensed that only water could oppose the coming redeemer, but they missed that form must overcome matter; throwing him into the water became a cause of the redemption, and he later split the sea.
The Flood, which wiped out all that has form through water, was delayed 120 years in the merit of Moshe, the embodiment of form, who would live 120 years.

Dasan, from 'das', stood against Moshe the giver of Torah, while Aviram, 'the father is great', stood against Aharon, whose holiness passes by inheritance; their opposition mirrors Moshe's spiritual greatness and Aharon's holiness of the body.
Because Moshe's third test concerned injustice among gentiles, the Torah he was chosen to give is a Torah of kindness for Israel and for all mankind.
Being born circumcised is not a mere wonder but a sign: the orlah expresses a share in evil and nature, and only one who came to the world solely to repair others could be born without it.

Malki-tzedek, himself born circumcised, could not prove from milah that man can improve on nature, so he made the point to Avraham with bread and wine, the two foods whose brachah rises when they are changed.
The aron is so named from 'or', light, yet Torah's light is felt only after the weeks of Shovavim have removed the orlah; then milah itself becomes a feast of joy rather than pain.
Water, which has no form of its own, is the opposite of Moshe, the pure form; the astrologers saw this but erred, since water ruled him only through the sin at Mei Merivah.
Moshe's marriage to a convert reflects his greatness: being above the six hundred thousand, his match had to be someone who also stood outside them.
Yisro's wandering through every idol was itself a sign of an all-inclusive soul, fitting him to be father-in-law to Moshe, who includes all Israel.
Yisro recognized Sarah's descendant precisely in Moshe not coming to collect thanks: modesty is the 'trademark' of Sarah's children, the source of blessing.
Since nature was made to serve the tzaddikim, a miracle for a tzaddik is barely a miracle; the true miracle is when Hashem breaks nature for someone who does not keep the Torah's own laws.
The same Torah that set how water behaves sets how a Jew should behave, so nature has a claim to keep its laws for someone who does not keep his.

The punishment of the wicked is a separate part of a miracle, not needed for the tzaddikim's survival, so even tzaddikim must sing over it; this is why the women sang only the verse about the horse and rider.

The Chasam Sofer's reading resolves Tosafos' question on the Rashbam: the women were the cause of the miracle precisely because they were tzaddikos, and for that reason they were only secondary in it.
The jar of man was kept in the Kodesh HaKodashim beside the Torah because emunah that Hashem provides is what allows a person to learn Torah instead of worrying about a livelihood.
The nachash's word 'hishiani' contains 'yesh ayin', the same doubt as 'hayesh Hashem b'kirbeinu im ayin' that brought Amalek.
Tu B'Shvat is a judgment for people too, since a person is compared to a tree: everyone is rooted in Hashem, but not everyone yields the fruit of mitzvos and good deeds.

The Mashgiach links 'kashin l'zavgan k'krias Yam Suf' to the hidden world: a shidduch is hard like Krias Yam Suf because both reveal the alma d'iskasya, which is why even the bas kol does not know the right match at first.
The bas kol could not identify who revealed the secrets of the Targum because Yonasan ben Uziel came from a world higher than the bas kol, and this is why his place is the place of shidduchim.
Targum, equal to tardeimah, goes down into the language of the nations to draw close hidden Jewish souls, and so the first Targum came from Onkelos the convert.
Yaakov took Leah, Esav's intended, from him, so he owed Esav a match, which explains why he was punished for hiding Dina.
Purim is a 'grabbed-away' Yom Tov, taken from Esav's months with tears, corresponding to Leah who took herself away from Esav with her tears.
Tehillim's 'He rebuked the Yam Suf' refers to the sea splitting a second time for Dasan and Aviram, who lacked Yosef's merit, so it had to be compelled.
Since 'ki va sus Paroh' is a forecast of the future Shirah at the second Krias Yam Suf, it is not part of the Shirah, as the Ramban says, yet it is written in the Shirah's layout.

The sea's refusal to split was not defiance of its condition: it sensed that this was not yet the time of universal joy, and Yosef's coffin, recalling 'Yosif Hashem shenis', told it that this splitting was only the first of two.

The twelve paths of the sea match the twelve notes of the octave, seven white and five black, because the splitting held both song for leaving Mitzrayim and weeping for the golus still ahead; the future seven paths match the seven pure notes.
Piano keys are called 'keys' because, as the Tikkunei Zohar teaches, niggun is what opens certain heavenly chambers.
Musical harmony is a shidduch made in Heaven: notes that belong together give pleasure as a good match does, and today's noisy music is the opposite of a shidduch, an expression of promiscuity.
The white keys are chesed and the black keys are din; the black notes are broken like the shevarim of the shofar, and only they can produce a sad niggun.
An eighth string on the future harp is not a small addition: as adding a digit multiplies the possible numbers, one more note will multiply music many times over into a song never yet heard.
The four avos nezikin are the four forces of tumah standing opposite the four letters of Hashem's Name, which the four parshiyos represent; tumah destroys where kedushah builds.
'Adam hamazik' is a contradiction in terms: a damager is not an adam, and Rav proves that maveh is a person from a teshuvah passuk because a damager earns the name adam only when he repents.
A person's possessions belong to his soul the way Chava belonged to Adam; that is why the same heavenly voice that assigns a wife also assigns a house and a field.
Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey was not a special animal; his own righteousness extended into it.
Each damager reflects a fault of the owner: keren his anger, shen his pursuit of pleasure, and regel, from 'ragil', his habits.
Kayin's complaint was that Hashem, the Shomer of the world, did not guard him; the Mashgiach turns this into the prayer that Hashem be one's guardian.

Every creature is a 'recipe' of one or more of the ten utterances, hidden behind its material form; the makkos made those hidden utterances visible, and the Zohar matches them in reverse, so Makas Bechoros reveals 'Bereishis' and Choshech undoes 'let there be light'.
Pharaoh's 'kaved' heart is a liver, which hardens the more it is cooked; this heartlessness, like the donkey that defied the king, was the vessel through which all the makkos came.

The Torah calls Egyptians 'those who feared the word of Hashem' only by Barad because Barad, the seventh makkah corresponding to Malchus, rained down real yiras Shamayim; when Pharaoh's plea cut it short, their fear left them, which is how they could chase the Jews with those same horses.

Moshe Rabbeinu's tefillah with spread hands outside the city was not for Mitzrayim but that the unfinished Barad remain suspended, so the Jews before Moshiach could draw yiras Shamayim from it, for example at shalosh seudos.
Every song is emunah, because song is harmony and conflicting thoughts are its opposite.

Barad fell on Rosh Chodesh Shevat, and Shevat and Shabbos are phonetically one; Shevat brings the new crop of Torah and Shabbos is the day of Torah, so Shevat, Torah, Shabbos and Barad are 'all cousins'.
The Barad that broke the trees of Mitzrayim was, for the Jews, the first stage of the blossoming of their own tree, the tree of Torah.
The makkos in Mitzrayim were a rerun of creation, replaying the ten maamaros in reverse, so that whoever did not witness the creation could see it in Mitzrayim.

The seven makkos of Va'eira match the seven midos and the three of Bo match chochmah, binah and da'as, like the six simanim with the ke'arah beneath them and the three matzos above on the seder plate.
The 'fear of Hashem's word' of some Egyptians at barad was not their own achievement but a flow of yiras Shamayim brought down by the plague of malchus, and it ended when the hail was stopped.
Moshe's unusual tefillah with outspread hands outside the city was not really for Pharaoh but for the Jews of the last generation, that the suspended hail should bring them yiras Shamayim.
Barad fell in Shevat, a month of yiras Shamayim that the Mashgiach links phonetically to Shabbos, and so Shevat already begins to usher in Moshiach.
The Mishnah's insistence on the date of the new year for trees prepares a farmer for the days of Moshiach, when the halacha will follow Beis Shammai retroactively.
The spilled wine at the Seder is the makkah of Mitzrayim and the refilled cup over which the Haggadah is said is the Jews' healing, so the very same act of the makkos is reenacted in two directions.
The fourth expression of redemption is set in a separate passuk for the same reason the chazir is: Edom, the fourth exile, outweighs all the others, and so does its redemption.
The ten makkos run backwards against the ten utterances: the last makkah, bechoros, undoes 'Bereishis', and the ninth, choshech, undoes 'yehi or'.

Barad is the Shabbos among the makkos, and since Shabbos is yiras Shamayim, the hail literally rained yiras Shamayim; the Egyptians' fear came from the hail and vanished when it stopped, which is why they later pursued the Jews.
Had Moshe Rabbeinu not been obliged to stop the barad at Pharaoh's plea, the yiras Shamayim it brought down would have restored the world to its state before Adam's sin and brought Moshiach.
The hail still suspended from Mitzrayim is what will fall in the war of Gog uMagog, a war against emunah, and shalosh seudos in the dark, emunah without seeing, protects from it.
The sea refused to split because its condition from creation was tied to the complete geulah; it split only when shown that the redemption had been divided in two.
The Midrash says the sea returned 'to its first condition' only when it closed, because by splitting at the Exodus it had not yet fulfilled its condition; it still awaits a second splitting.
'The sea saw and fled' mirrors Yosef who 'fled and went outside': Yosef escaped the moment he would lose his free choice, and Hashem, measure for measure, rescued Israel at that same point.

Yosef promised more than Yaakov asked: since a son's bones are his father's, not burying himself in Egypt completed Yaakov's own burial, and calling himself 'bones' stressed that it was all for his father's honor.
Beis Shammai, being sharper, sensed the new year of trees already on the first of Shevat, while Beis Hillel sensed it only on the fifteenth.
The sea saw in Yosef's bones the life of Yaakov carried on in his son, the proof that Klal Yisrael never dies; the same life underlies the Tu BiShvat tree.
The prohibition of returning to Egypt explains why the miracle had to happen at the sea: a brachah on a miracle is made at its place, and only a place outside Egypt could be visited to make it.
The Shabbos cholent, though by nature an unhealthy dish, carries a trace of the mann, since Shabbos food prepared on Erev Shabbos draws the blessing that rested on the mann.
Laws, decrees and takanos come from the Sages, but minhagim rise from the people, even the simple folk, out of the ruach hakodesh hidden in the collective of Klal Yisroel.
The names of border cities are expounded because each border hints that every tribe and every person has his own boundary of parnassa that no one else can cross.

Shira is said only for what is above nature; since nature exists to protect the tzaddik, the righteous women's rescue was natural, and only the Egyptians' downfall was a miracle for them, which is why Miriam sang just that one passuk.

The Rambam and Raavad do not argue in principle: the Rambam cites Yeshayahu, which sets no condition of righteousness, while the Raavad cites Bechukosai, which promises the end of wild beasts only if the Torah is kept, as the Ramban explains.
By not requiring wonders, the Rambam demands more of Moshiach: Eliyahu's fire from heaven did not change the people for long, while Moshiach will move every Jew to leave everything by his word alone.
The Mashgiach calls the parsha itself a mikveh: just as one immerses in water, one must immerse oneself in the sea of emunah that the parsha holds.
The sunrise is no less a miracle than the mann; people only take it for granted because they are used to it, while the mann had no habit behind it, so trusting it was pure emunah.
Since the last line of a letter sums it up, the last passuk of Tehillim, read with Chazal as thanks for every breath, is the summary of the whole sefer.
Amalek, the doubt at Masa and the serpent's seduction of Chava are one force: doubt that enters a Jew's mind and makes him question whether Hashem is among us.
Not being ashamed while davening is not brazenness; it means being so absorbed that one does not know where one is or that people are watching.
A segulah is like a free remedy whose workings no one can explain, yet it can achieve what costly medicines do; the Sefer Charedim's segulos atone for sin without the cost of fasts and afflictions.
The donkey, the most physical of creatures, is far from holiness, yet Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's holiness reached even it; this is the measure of repair demanded at the end of Shovavim.
'Adam hamazik' is a contradiction in terms, since a true person does not damage; the term can only mean the man who repairs his damage, which is why the Gemara's proof for it is a passuk of teshuvah.
Kayin's 'am I my brother's keeper' is read as a complaint that Hashem is the guardian of the world; his failing was that he did not appoint Hashem as his own guardian.
The 'shomer' of the passuk from which the Gemara learns that mav'eh is adam is Hashem, the guardian of one who does teshuvah.
The Mishnah's unusual first-person 'hichsharti' hints that when a person's ox damages, his own anger, appetite and bad habits are responsible.
Statements of extreme severity in the Zohar or the Rambam, absent from the Gemara, are addressed to people of a high level, for whom a small flaw is like an ink spot on a silk shirt.
The last passuk of Yisro is derush, but by Mishpatim, after Shovavim, its demand against arrogance becomes din, as hinted in 'these are the laws'.

Moshe not entering Eretz Yisrael was itself the reward for his mesiras nefesh: because he would not lead the war, the generation of the desert and later Klal Yisrael were saved, since Hashem poured His wrath on wood and stones.

Avraham gave water through a messenger out of chesed: hating avodah zarah intensely, he let someone else wash the guests' feet so they would not feel his irritation, and measure for measure Klal Yisrael received water in the desert through Moshe, which spared them.
Pharaoh's 'I made myself' and the claim that the world made itself are one position: the source of creation lies within the creature itself, so that the creation and the creator are the same.
The greatest wonder of the Exodus was that the Egyptians, after all the wonders, still denied; the Torah records this because the same Pharaoh lives in every person.

Following the Satmar Rav, the limbs of a holy person become a vessel for their counterparts above, so an eye or heart without fear of Hashem is only an organ, not truly an eye or a heart; this is the meaning of the Midrash that Pharaoh had no heart.

The souls of the generation of Mitzrayim, to whom 'veheveisi' was promised but not fulfilled, return in the generation before Moshiach: they did not believe when they saw, and now they believe without seeing.

The Mashgiach reads Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's 'go to Negaim and Ohalos' as a hint: those tractates of the gravest tumah open with 'shnayim', showing that tumah cannot start from 'one', and so the frog plague could not have grown from a single mother frog.

Since the frog is a partnership of pure and impure, neither one root frog nor two frogs fits; Rabbi Elazar's whistle, one calling and many coming, expresses the yachid and the rabim together, the mixture itself.
The frog's song is the only one in Perek Shirah that is not a passuk, because it is the song sung from the beis hakisei, where a passuk may not be said, and it must be said quietly.

Each impure species has a pure counterpart on land or in the sea that serves as its shliach tzibbur for song, but the dog, impure in both, has none, which is why its song needed a special merit: its tongue.
The dog's lowliness is its total nullification to a human master; its song 'come let us bow before Hashem' is the future tikun of that trait, bowing to Hashem instead.
Hotza'ah on Shabbos is a mixing of the reshus of the One with the reshus of the many, which is why Maseches Shabbos opens with 'yetzios haShabbos shtayim'.

Beis Shammai's Rosh Hashanah for trees on Rosh Chodesh Shevat is not a disagreement with Beis Hillel but a finer perception: the renewal of the Jewish soul, Hashem's tree, begins then, and only the sharper great ones feel it already on Rosh Chodesh.
Shevat is related to 'judging', since beis and pei interchange: in Shevat each person is judged on how he can adapt to the new Torah and the new conduct that come down.

The title 'one who feared the word of Hashem' belongs to someone who breaks his klipah to follow the tzaddik, not to someone who protected his animals because experience at the pestilence taught him Moshe was right.
The hail, the seventh plague, corresponds to the seventh commandment from the top, Shabbos, and to malchus; therefore it came in Shevat, which the Chasam Sofer reads as Shabbos.

Moshe's prayer to stop the hail was really a prayer for the Jews of the last generation: that the unfallen hail stay suspended as a reserve of yiras shamayim for the war against emunah before Moshiach.
Moshe had to leave the city and spread his hands only at the hail because a prayer for Jews' emunah draws many accusers, while a salvation for a goy, as at the frogs, is easy.

The Jews said 'Hashem will reign' and not 'Hashem reigns' because Pharaoh's horses survived the hail through God-fearing Egyptians: the hail had not come down in full, so the redemption was not yet complete.
The Mashgiach says the depth of the Maharal does not come from sharpness or constructions; the sweetness is that once explained, it is seen to be simple truth.
A 'sechel nivdal' is a mind whose only drive is to know what Hashem says in His Torah, free of the biases that every person's experiences leave on his reasoning.
Six hundred thousand reflects six in units, hundreds and thousands, and six is completeness: a body with four sides, a top and a bottom.
Galus is always to the opposite of what Yisrael are, so the depth of their fall, as with the daughter of Nakdimon ben Gurion, reveals their height; this is 'ashreichem Yisrael'.
A beginning is the 'one', not the 'five'; it must come out of nothing, so Avraham was born as the two thousand years of tohu ended, just as light comes when darkness ends.
Avraham was to the Jewish people what Adam was to mankind: a new species whose tie to Terach was cut, which is why Rashi says he was freed from honoring his father.

A shidduch comes from the hidden world and is too lofty to descend into this world on its own; the shadchan's untruth gives it the 'lowering' it needs, which is why the Divrei Chaim paid even shadchanim whose matches failed.

A bas kol, lower than prophecy, cannot grasp what belongs to the hidden world; therefore it announces wrong matches before the right one, and therefore it did not know that Yonasan ben Uziel had revealed its secrets.

Leah belonged to the hidden world like Esav, while Rachel belonged to the revealed world; her tears, which changed her mazal, were themselves a revelation of the hidden world like the splitting of the sea.

The repeated 'uvnei Yisrael halchu bayabasha' after the sea closed refers to Dasan and Aviram crossing later, which reconciles the Ibn Ezra and the Ramban: it is a Shirah, but that of Dasan and Aviram, not of all Israel.
Following the Rama MiFano, the two bulls of Eliyahu were Dasan and Aviram, and their tikkun comes at Ne'ilah of Yom Kippur, the peak of achdus, when their verse 'Hashem hu haElokim' is called out.
Acharon shel Pesach is called 'acharon', the last, because on it even the last and most lost Jew can be raised.

Just as the Satan provoked the two men's quarrel specifically on erev Shabbos to keep Shabbos, which is peace, from entering, so the machlokes of today comes because history stands at the erev Shabbos before Moshiach.
